\begin{abstract}
Cylinder chess joins the a-file to the h-file, so the board has no edges or corners. We study its
king-and-pawn endgames with combinatorial game theory after Elkies: a passed pawn wins, and the kings are
frozen in a mutual zugzwang worth zero. We repair this model with a passed-pawn test that respects en
passant, and say when the frozen kings are exact. Under the new
test and the count rule, an exhaustive scan finds no nimber above star with at most six pawns on ordinary boards of any
width, but star two appears with seven, in one position and its color-reversed twin, whose values three
programs confirm; on the three-file cylinder six pawns suffice, and on seven files ten-pawn rings reach star three.
We find king-and-pawn positions worth one-eighth, up-second star and Tiny 1; with frozen kings and queen
promotions only, the one-eighth survives in real chess. Tablebases
confirm that king and rook cannot force mate on the cylinder, where opposite-colored bishops still
can. We correct earlier work on cylinder Dawson's chess: the full ring is a first-player win exactly when the
strip three files shorter has Grundy value zero.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Chess, combinatorial game theory, endgame tablebases, game solving, nimbers.
\end{IEEEkeywords}
